newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss rule out apology over Holocaust records.
newsitem.headline: Swiss rule out apology over Holocaust records.

text.p: The Swiss government sees no need to apologise to a watchman who left the country fearing for his safety after saving Holocaust-era documents from shredding at Switzerland's biggest bank, President Arnold Koller said.

Koller said in an interview with the national daily tabloid Blick published on Thursday that the government had no influence over Zurich prosecutors who are investigating whether security guard Christoph Meili or Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) broke the law.

The interview appeared one day after U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato demanded the Swiss president and UBS apologise to Meili, who fled to the United States after saying he felt threatened for blowing the whistle at UBS.
"There is no reason to do so (apologise)," Koller told Blick when asked about the demand.
"Under our system of separation of state powers, Meili's case is in the hands of Zurich prosecutors," he added.
"The separation of powers is something that is also well respected in the United States, by the way," he added.
UBS declined to comment on the demand for an apology.
It said it had repeatedly voiced regret over the shredding incident, which it has called a mistake by the bank's chief archivist rather than a deliberate act by bank directors.
"We have said from the beginning that the shredding was a regrettable error and not our intention," UBS spokeswoman Gertrud Erismann told Reuters.
The Federal Banking Commission, the Swiss bank regulator, accepted UBS's version of events after demanding a report.

Meili, a 28-year-old night watchman, caused world headlines in January when he took documents from a UBS shredder room that came from a subsidiary Swiss bank bought by UBS in 1945, Eidgenoesische Bank (Eiba).
Meili gave the records to a Zurich Jewish group which handed them to prosecutors, who launched two criminal investigations.

One probe is into whether Meili broke bank secrecy laws and the other is into UBS broke a federal law protecting documents that could help a sweeping inquiry by historians into the Swiss financial role in World War Two.

The international panel of historians carrying out the wartime probe said this month the files, including records of pre-1945 properties in Germany, were relevant to its work and therefore fell under the federal protection decree.
Meili, his wife and two young children became permanent U.S. residents on Tuesday after President Bill Clinton signed a bill sponsored by D'Amato.
D'Amato said on Tuesday he would consider "severe penalties" against Switzerland if an apology to Meili was not forthcoming.

D'Amato said those penalties could include an inquiry into whether Switzerland had violated two accords between the Allied powers of the Second World War and Switzerland with regard to turning over all German accounts from its banks.
According to D'Amato, other possible penalties include U.S. federal or state reviews of UBS's authority to operate in the United States, the world's biggest financial market.
Swiss bankers said D'Amato's threats could not be taken lightly because the New York senator, who heads the Senate Banking Commission, was seeking reelection next year.
"There is a widespread view that he is doing this for his reelection campaign," said one banker, who declined to be named, about D'Amato's repeated attacks against Swiss banks.
